title: The Art of War
blurb: Sun Tzu’s 2,500-year-old book on strategy, in four short episodes.

sources.title: The Art of War, translated by Lionel Giles (Project Gutenberg)

cards.text: A Chinese book on strategy, traditionally credited to the general Sun Tzu and usually dated to around the 5th century BC. It has 13 short chapters.
The art of war is of vital importance to the State.
Before any campaign, Sun Tzu weighs five factors: the Moral Law (whether people are united behind their leader), Heaven, Earth, the Commander, and Method and discipline.
All warfare is based on deception.
Its real subject is strategy: how to win at the least cost. That’s why people in business, sport and politics still read it.

cards.q: How many chapters does The Art of War have?

points: A book on strategy from ancient China
Winning at the least cost is the aim

cards.text: Sun Tzu’s best-known idea is that the finest way to win is without a battle at all.
Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.
Long campaigns drain money, supplies and morale, so Sun Tzu warns against drawn-out wars.
There is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare.
In war, then, let your great object be victory, not lengthy campaigns.

cards.q: For Sun Tzu, supreme excellence is…
cards.explain: Breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.

points: The best win needs no battle
Aim for a quick, decisive result

cards.text: Sun Tzu puts knowledge at the centre of strategy: understand your own strengths and weaknesses, and your opponent’s.
If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.
He goes on: know yourself but not the enemy, and every victory comes with a defeat; know neither, and you’ll lose every battle.
The last chapter is about spies. For Sun Tzu, good information is worth far more than it costs.

cards.q: What does Sun Tzu say you need, to fear no battle?
opts: To know the enemy and yourself
cards.explain: To know the enemy and to know yourself.

points: Good information is worth paying for

cards.text: Sun Tzu compares an army to water, which avoids high ground, flows to low places and takes its shape from the land.
Water shapes its course according to the nature of the ground over which it flows; the soldier works out his victory in relation to the foe whom he is facing.
Appear at points which the enemy must hasten to defend; march swiftly to places where you are not expected.
In modern terms: study the field and your rivals, choose contests you can win, go where others aren’t, and adapt as things change.

cards.q: What does Sun Tzu compare a good army to?
cards.explain: Water, which adapts its course to the ground.

points: Adapt to the situation, like water
